tier_reason: First-party BenchmarkDotNet code is public (src/Pfim.Benchmarks/TargaBenchmark.cs, DdsBenchmark.cs, BaseConfig.cs) and every number in the record matches analysis/TargaBenchmark-report.csv and DdsBenchmark-report.csv (Mean, ns), but no CPU model is recorded anywhere and the CSVs come from an April 2019 run that has not been repeated, so C.

corrections.baseline: FreeImage (via FreeImage-dotnet-core 4.3.6 with a bundled FreeImage.dll), DevIL (via DevILSharp 0.2.4) and ImageMagick (via Magick.NET-Q16-AnyCPU 7.12.0), all native C/C++ libraries driven from .NET, plus managed Targa decoders TargaImage 1.0, ImageFormats 1.0, StbSharp 0.7.2.38 and TgaSharpLib 1.0
corrections.compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet 0.11.5, net461 target (.NET Framework 4.6.1; CSV shows Runtime=Clr, Jit=RyuJit, Platform=X64), PlatformTarget AnyCPU, Release build (benchmark project as of commit 6bdf779, April 2019); CSV times are nanoseconds (BaseConfig exports TimeUnit.Nanosecond, analysis.R converts ns to microseconds). The current csproj (net8.0, BenchmarkDotNet 0.15.6, Magick.NET 14.9.1, DevILSharp 0.2.20, FreeImage.Standard 4.3.8) has not been re-run.
corrections.workload: Decoding one 120x120 image from an in-memory byte[] in 3 Targa variants (24-bit RLE, 32-bit RLE, 32-bit raw) and 4 DDS variants (32-bit, DXT1, DXT3, DXT5), measured with BenchmarkDotNet as mean time per decode; Pfim decodes with a pooled ArrayPool allocator (PfimAllocator) that reuses the output buffer, the other libraries allocate a fresh image per call.
corrections.caveats: One 120x120 test image per format, so per-call fixed costs dominate. No CPU model anywhere in the repo. The CSVs were committed on 2019-04-20 (Pfim 0.7.0 era, .NET Framework 4.6.1, DevILSharp 0.2.4); a 2022 README edit relabelled the contestants as Pfim 0.10.0 and DevIL 0.2.19 without new data, so the README version list does not describe the measured run. Unequal work: the Pfim benchmark passes a pooled ArrayPool allocator, so its output buffer is reused (312 B allocated per Targa decode versus 5,361 B for FreeImage and 343,195 B for TargaImage in the CSV), and Pfim's own 0.7.0 release notes say naive pooling gives up to a 3x speedup in these benchmarks; the FreeImage benchmark returns the FreeImageBitmap without disposing it (native memory reclaimed by finalizers, Gen 2 collections in its row); ImageMagick runs the Q16 build (16-bit-per-channel pixel cache) and native libraries are reached through .NET interop wrappers whose marshalling cost is included. README claim 'more than 10x faster than the closest competitor' does not hold for 24bit-rle.tga against DevILSharp (9.4x, derived from page data); for DDS Pfim leads FreeImage by 1.61x on DXT1 and 1.16x on DXT3 and is 1.1% slower on DXT5 (derived from page data). Baselines are not libjpeg-turbo/libpng/libwebp/libavif, so the result says little about mainstream codecs.

notes: Numbers verified against both CSVs. The measured Pfim path uses a pooled allocator that the competitors do not get, and the CSV predates the README's stated versions by about three years; kept at C with those shortcomings.

tier_reason: The README table (36.324 vs 5.150, 127.034 vs 24.857, 0.159 vs 0.029 ops/s) matches the JMH results recorded in src/test/java/com/pngencoder/PngEncoderBenchmarkPngEncoderVsImageIO.java (commit 5cc8d61, 2020-09-17), but CPU model, JDK version and JVM flags are not stated and the run is the project's own, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: JMH harness PngEncoderBenchmarkPngEncoderVsImageIO.java: Mode.Throughput, 1 fork, 1 warmup iteration of 2 s, 1 measurement iteration of 5 s, 1 benchmark thread when the README table was recorded (2020-09-17; an 8-thread runner was added in 2022). JDK version and JVM flags not stated (project compiles for Java 8, Travis CI used openjdk8; current pom uses JMH 1.37).
corrections.workload: Encoding BufferedImages to a null OutputStream: a random 1024x1024 TYPE_INT_ARGB image, a 2121x350 logo and a 4900x6000 Looklet photograph converted to TYPE_INT_ARGB; PngEncoder at its default deflate level 9 with predictor (row filter) encoding off and multithreaded segment compression on a pool of availableProcessors threads, against ImageIO.write(image, "png", OutputStream) with default parameters; reported as images encoded per second.
corrections.caveats: Speedup comes mainly from multithreading: PngEncoder compresses segments on a fixed pool of availableProcessors threads while ImageIO compresses on one thread, and the README says a single-core machine sees no significant gain; a 2022 commit adding an 8-benchmark-thread mode is titled 'Add benchmark for multiple threads. ImageIO gains more :(' and publishes no numbers. The work differs: PngEncoder by default writes scanlines without row filtering, while ImageIO runs adaptive per-row filter selection; ImageIO's deflate level is 9 on JDK 8 (Deflater.BEST_COMPRESSION in jdk8u PNGImageWriter) but 4 on JDK 9 and later (DEFAULT_COMPRESSION_LEVEL = 4), and the JDK used is not stated. The harness calls ImageIO.write on an OutputStream without ImageIO.setUseCache(false), so by JDK default (useCache = true) the ImageIO side writes through a FileCacheImageOutputStream temp file. The benchmark does not record output sizes; the README only says multithreaded output is about 2% larger than ImageIO's. One 5 s measurement iteration with no error estimate; the 4900x6000 case runs at 0.029 ops/s for ImageIO (about 34 s per encode, derived from page data), so that figure rests on about one encode. CPU model ('8 logical cores' only) and JDK not stated; first-party benchmark. Lowering the compression level to 1 gives 2.31x more speed for 2.50x larger files per the README speed-versus-size table. Baseline is the JDK ImageIO writer, not libpng; the Java wrapper fpng-java (not reported here) reports much larger gains over ImageIO by calling the native fpng library. Commits since the 0.16.0 release (2025-05-19) are dependency bumps only.

notes: Numbers verified in README and benchmark source comment (initial 2020-08-17 run gave 6.0x/5.2x/5.6x). Confirmed at C; shortcomings are parallel versus single-threaded encoding, unfiltered versus adaptive-filtered rows, JDK-dependent ImageIO deflate level and ImageIO's default temp-file cache. Last commit corrected to 2025-11-25 (active).

tier_reason: Upgraded from D: the README has no numbers, but the project's own PR #705 (2026-03-15 comment, table repeated in issue #724) gives libjxl vs jxl-rs MP/s for 8 images measured single-threaded on an AMD EPYC 9645 (AVX-512); first-party, libjxl build and harness not stated, no public script runs both decoders, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'The performance of jxl-rs closely matches (and sometimes exceeds) the C++ reference implementation' (no numbers). PR #705 comment by hjanuschka (2026-03-15, repeated in issue #724), single-threaded, AMD EPYC 9645 (AVX-512), jxl-rs built with PGO, libjxl vs jxl-rs in MP/s: sunset_logo (modular) 6.31 vs 7.05 (1.12x), bike (VarDCT) 39.48 vs 36.69 (0.93x), green_queen_modular 8.99 vs 11.42 (1.27x), green_queen_vardct 35.83 vs 33.56 (0.94x), bicycles (modular+WP) 14.91 vs 12.05 (0.81x), delta_palette 10.60 vs 11.15 (1.05x), lz77_flower 3.52 vs 4.38 (1.24x), patches_lossless 13.81 vs 14.30 (1.04x), total 15.74 vs 16.35 MP/s (1.04x). Earlier draft PR #506 (2025-12-01) reported '30/39 conformance tests pass (2.23x avg vs C++)' and '6 tests faster than C++' (for example bike 226.15 ms Rust vs 163.10 ms C++).
corrections.workload: Single-threaded decoding of 8 JPEG XL test images (sunset_logo, bike, green_queen modular and VarDCT, bicycles, delta_palette, lz77_flower, patches_lossless), throughput in MP/s, on the unmerged PR #705 branch; jxl_cli --speedtest measures jxl-rs alone and the libjxl command line and repetition count are not stated.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: jxl-rs: PGO + AVX-512 per the PR #705 comments; repo release profile lto = "thin", panic = "abort"; rustc version, RUSTFLAGS and the libjxl build flags not stated.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are first-party (project collaborator hjanuschka) from PR #705, which maintainer veluca93 asked to split because it carried a lot of unsafe code and which was closed unmerged on 2026-09-03; its optimizations were re-landed through separate PRs tracked in issue #724, so current main may not reproduce the table. No public script measures libjxl and jxl-rs together: the CI benchmark (jxl-perfhistory in .github/workflows/pull_request.yml) compares a PR with its base only. jxl-rs is slower on the lossy VarDCT images that dominate web use (0.93x, 0.94x) and on bicycles (0.81x) and faster on modular/lossless images; the 1.04x total comes from a PGO build. Issue #803 (i5-12400, 2026-06-13) shows -Ctarget-cpu=native cutting a lossless modular decode from 14.757 to 7.895 MP/s, so build flags change results. A WebSearch snippet from a third-party article (page not opened, snippet only) says the Rust decoder 'performs within 15 to 25% of the C++ reference implementation's speed'. A separate WebSearch snippet about tirr-c/jxl-oxide (another Rust decoder) said djxl ran about 2.80x faster than jxl-oxide, so Rust decoders do not uniformly match libjxl.

notes: Orchestrator asked to confirm no number exists: numbers do exist in PR #705 and issue #724 (and older PR #506), so the entry moves from D to C with the CPU stated; parity overall, slower on VarDCT. Metadata (BSD-3-Clause, 712 stars, last commit 2026-10-03) checked and unchanged.
